passage: I'm Sharmila. I read my list of ten things for the science kit before bed, then checked against it and found I had forgotten two. That felt bad. So I covered the list with my copybook and tried to say every item aloud. I got seven. I peeked and tried again. Nine. Again. This time I said all ten, even the boring ones: the ruler and the plastic cups. Francis, my cousin, was listening from the sofa and clapped when I was done. Then I put the list away, went to sleep, and in the morning I could still say them all before breakfast.

Tuition teacher's note, Tuesday
Anjali had a list of eight things to bring for Wednesday's model-making class. I asked her to read it once, then close her notebook and tell me. She said six. The glue gun sticks and the thermocol were missing, and she was annoyed with herself. Instead of reading it again, she covered the list with her palm and tried to say the whole thing. Seven. She peeked, covered it again. Eight. She did it twice more until she could say all eight three times without a mistake. At the end she said, "I'll say it once before sleeping." Today she came with all eight things. I have started using her cover-and-say trick with the younger group.
- Parul

qa.q: Which two items did Anjali miss the first time?
qa.a: The glue gun sticks and the thermocol.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel when she found she had missed two items?
qa.a: She was annoyed with herself, which pushed her to test herself properly.

qa.q: What other approach could Anjali use if she is short of time?
qa.a: She could write the two items she forgets most on her hand or a sticky note, because it targets exactly the weak spots.

qa.q: How does the cover-and-say trick look to Parul?
qa.a: Parul finds it useful enough to start using it with the younger group.

grounding: It shows a girl who missed two items covering the list and repeating it until she gets them all, and then sleeping on it.

Sunday
Dear diary, the Monday checklist for the swimming class has ten things. Last Monday I forgot my goggles AND my towel and had to drip-dry like a wet cat. Mahima laughed so hard. So tonight I did something new. I read the list, then covered it with my geometry box and said it all. Nine. Towel again! I checked, covered, said it again. Ten, but slowly. Then again. Ten, fast. Then Mahima tested me from the bed, jumping about the order: "Okay, clever girl, what comes after the soap?" "Cap." I got it. Now I'm going to sleep and say it once more in the morning before we leave. Fingers crossed. No wet cat tomorrow.
- Jasleen

qa.a: Jasleen felt embarrassed, especially when Mahima laughed, and wanted to avoid it happening again.

qa.q: How does the evening look to Mahima?
qa.a: Mahima enjoys testing Jasleen from the bed and turns it into a game, probably feeling playful and helpful.
